about.description:
The Porous Microstructure Analysis (PuMA) software has been developed to compute effective material properties and perform material response simulations on digitized microstructures of porous media. PuMA is able to import digital three-dimensional images obtained from X-ray microtomography or to generate artificial microstructures that mimic real materials. PuMA also provides a module for interactive 3D visualizations. Version 3 includes modules to compute simple morphological properties such as porosity, volume fractions, pore diameter, and specific surface area. Additional capabilities include the determination of effective thermal and electrical conductivity (both radiative and solid conduction - including the ability to simulate local anisotropy for the latter); effective diffusivity and tortuosity from the continuum to the rarefied regime; techniques to determine the local material orientation, as well as the mechanical properties (elasticity coefficient), and the permeability of a material. Some examples of microstructures that have been run in the past are shown in the pictures below, together with PuMA's software architecture schematic.

### Citing PuMA If you use PuMA in your research, please use the following BibTeX entries to cite it: ```BibTeX @article{puma2021, title={Update 3.0 to "PuMA: The Porous Microstructure Analysis software",(PII: S2352711018300281)}, author={Ferguson, Joseph C and Semeraro, Federico and Thornton, John M and Panerai, Francesco and Borner, Arnaud and Mansour, Nagi N}, journal={SoftwareX}, volume={15}, pages={100775}, year={2021}, publisher={Elsevier} } @article{puma2018, title={PuMA: The porous microstructure analysis software}, author={Ferguson, Joseph C and Panerai, Francesco and Borner, Arnaud and Mansour, Nagi N}, journal={SoftwareX}, volume={7}, pages={81--87}, year={2018}, publisher={Elsevier} } ```

raw_meta_yaml:
schema_version: 1 context: version: "3.2.2" build: 4 recipe: name: puma-split version: ${{ version }} source: url: https://github.com/nasa/puma/archive/refs/tags/v${{ version }}.tar.gz sha256: 25308c057b36a7d394a58f3b16ede621ba739b5c504e51c069edc913f086ad7d patches: # Cython's numpy.pxd dropped int_t, so the three .pyx files that declare # "ctypedef np.int_t DTYPE_t" no longer cythonize. intp_t is the indexing # type these arrays actually hold. - patches/numpy2-compatibility.patch # PuMA asks for --std=c++0x, which is C++11. Eigen 3.4 needs C++14 and # Eigen 5 needs C++17, so the library is compiled at C++17 instead. That # also means swapit.h can no longer declare its locals "register", which # C++17 removed: gcc only warns, but clang rejects it, and the header is # installed into the prefix, so it broke the GUI build and would break any # consumer compiling against libpuma. - patches/cxx17-standard.patch build: number: ${{ build + 100 * (microarch_level | default("1") | int - 1) }} outputs: # The C++ library on its own. It links fftw, libtiff and OpenMP and nothing # else, so keeping python out of this output is what lets the GUI below build # once per platform instead of once per python version. - package: name: libpuma build: # cpp/ is built with cmake, which this branch does not wire up for # Windows. skip: win script: build_libpuma requirements: build: - if: unix and x86_64 then: x86_64-microarch-level ==${{ microarch_level }} - ${{ compiler('c') }} - ${{ stdlib('c') }} - ${{ compiler('cxx') }} - if: linux then: libgomp - if: osx then: llvm-openmp - cmake <4 - make host: - eigen - fftw - libtiff tests: - script: - pumaX_testing 1 about: license: NASA-1.3 license_file: LICENSE.txt summary: PuMA C++ library. # pumapy links nothing from libPuMA, so it carries the python variants on its # own. It is built once per license family: the gpl build bundles TexGen, the # default build leaves it out. The build string names which one you have, the # way ffmpeg distinguishes its gpl and lgpl builds. - package: name: pumapy build: # TexGen needs swig and cmake, neither of which this branch wires up for # Windows, so only the permissive build exists there. skip: win and license_family == "gpl" # Resolution prefers the highest build number, so the permissive build is # offset above the gpl one to make it the default; ffmpeg does the same in # reverse to default to its gpl build. The offset has to clear the 100 per # microarch level the top-level number already uses. number: ${{ build + 100 * (microarch_level | default("1") | int - 1) + (1000 if license_family == "nasa" else 0) }} string: ${{ license_family }}_${{ hash }}_${{ build_number }} script: file: build_pumapy env: # rattler-build does not scan build scripts for variant keys, so the # family has to be handed to the script explicitly. PUMA_LICENSE_FAMILY: ${{ license_family }} requirements: build: - if: build_platform != target_platform then: - python - cross-python_${{ target_platform }} - cython - numpy - if: unix and x86_64 then: x86_64-microarch-level ==${{ microarch_level }} - ${{ compiler('c') }} - ${{ stdlib('c') }} - ${{ compiler('cxx') }} # Only TexGen needs these, so the default build does without them. - if: license_family == "gpl" and not win then: - cmake <4 - make - swig host: - python - cython - pip - setuptools - numpy run: - python - scipy >=1.11,<2 - scikit-image >=0.17 - matplotlib-base - pyvista >=0.46.5 - vtk - if: not win then: scikit-umfpack - if: linux then: ocl-icd-system tests: - python: imports: - if: license_family == "gpl" then: TexGen.Core - pumapy pip_check: false - script: - cd python/test && python -m unittest test_workspace.TestWorkspace files: source: - python/test/*.py about: license: ${{ "NASA-1.3 AND GPL-2.0-or-later" if license_family == "gpl" else "NASA-1.3" }} license_file: - LICENSE.txt - if: license_family == "gpl" then: install/TexGen/LICENSE.txt summary: ${{ "The pumapy python package, with the GPL TexGen bindings." if license_family == "gpl" else "The pumapy python package." }} # The GUI is a separate qmake build that links against the libPuMA installed # by the libpuma output, so libpuma is a host dependency rather than a shared # build step. Qt therefore only ever reaches this output. - package: name: puma build: skip: win script: build_puma requirements: build: - if: unix and x86_64 then: x86_64-microarch-level ==${{ microarch_level }} - ${{ compiler('c') }} - ${{ stdlib('c') }} - ${{ compiler('cxx') }} - if: linux then: libgomp - if: osx then: llvm-openmp - make host: - if: linux then: - xorg-libxfixes - libgl-devel - ${{ pin_subpackage('libpuma', exact=True) }} - eigen - fftw - libtiff - if: qt_major == "5" then: qt-main - if: qt_major == "6" then: - qt6-main - qt6-3d run: - ${{ pin_subpackage('libpuma', exact=True) }} tests: - script: # The test environment is headless, so Qt's default xcb plugin has no # display to connect to; offscreen is conda-forge's documented # substitute. pumaGUI ends in QApplication::exec() and never returns on # its own, so timeout stops it and --preserve-status reports the # resulting SIGTERM as 143. - QT_QPA_PLATFORM=offscreen timeout --preserve-status 10 pumaGUI || [[ $? -eq 143 ]] requirements: run: - coreutils about: # The GUI plots through the vendored QCustomPlot, which is GPL-3.0. license: NASA-1.3 AND GPL-3.0-or-later license_file: - LICENSE.txt - gui/src/Utilities/qcustomplot/GPL.txt summary: Desktop GUI for PuMA. about: homepage: https://github.com/nasa/puma license: NASA-1.3 license_file: - LICENSE.txt - install/TexGen/LICENSE.txt - gui/src/Utilities/qcustomplot/GPL.txt summary: A package to compute material properties from micro-CT data. description: | The Porous Microstructure Analysis (PuMA) software has been developed to compute effective material properties and perform material response simulations on digitized microstructures of porous media. PuMA is able to import digital three-dimensional images obtained from X-ray microtomography or to generate artificial microstructures that mimic real materials. PuMA also provides a module for interactive 3D visualizations. Version 3 includes modules to compute simple morphological properties such as porosity, volume fractions, pore diameter, and specific surface area. Additional capabilities include the determination of effective thermal and electrical conductivity (both radiative and solid conduction - including the ability to simulate local anisotropy for the latter); effective diffusivity and tortuosity from the continuum to the rarefied regime; techniques to determine the local material orientation, as well as the mechanical properties (elasticity coefficient), and the permeability of a material. Some examples of microstructures that have been run in the past are shown in the pictures below, together with PuMA's software architecture schematic.

### Citing PuMA If you use PuMA in your research, please use the following BibTeX entries to cite it: ```BibTeX @article{puma2021, title={Update 3.0 to "PuMA: The Porous Microstructure Analysis software",(PII: S2352711018300281)}, author={Ferguson, Joseph C and Semeraro, Federico and Thornton, John M and Panerai, Francesco and Borner, Arnaud and Mansour, Nagi N}, journal={SoftwareX}, volume={15}, pages={100775}, year={2021}, publisher={Elsevier} } @article{puma2018, title={PuMA: The porous microstructure analysis software}, author={Ferguson, Joseph C and Panerai, Francesco and Borner, Arnaud and Mansour, Nagi N}, journal={SoftwareX}, volume={7}, pages={81--87}, year={2018}, publisher={Elsevier} } ``` documentation: https://puma-nasa.readthedocs.io/ repository: https://gitlab.com/jcfergus/puma-dev extra: # The recipe is named puma-split because it produces several packages, so the # feedstock it belongs to has to be named explicitly. feedstock-name: puma recipe-maintainers: - fedesemeraro - Tobias-Fischer - joseph-ferguson - EricAtORS
